title: Complications of Musculoskeletal Problems
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction to Musculoskeletal Complications
headings.content: Musculoskeletal injuries, particularly fractures and severe trauma, present significant challenges in nursing care due to their potential for serious complications. When bones break or soft tissues are severely damaged, local and systemic disruptions can cascade rapidly, threatening patient survival and long-term functional recovery. As nursing students in Nigeria preparing for professional examinations, it is vital to understand that musculoskeletal complications are broadly categorized into early and late occurrences. Early complications, such as hypovolemic shock, fat embolism syndrome, and compartment syndrome, manifest within hours to days of the injury and require immediate, life-saving interventions. Late complications, including avascular necrosis, delayed union, malunion, nonunion, and chronic osteomyelitis, develop over weeks or months, often leading to prolonged physical disability, chronic pain, and extensive rehabilitation needs. Recognizing the pathophysiology behind these complications allows the nurse to anticipate risks, perform targeted physical assessments, and collaborate effectively with the multidisciplinary healthcare team. Prompt identification of subtle warning signs can prevent catastrophic outcomes and drastically improve patient prognosis. Furthermore, comprehensive nursing care involves continuous monitoring of vital signs, neurovascular status, and surgical sites, alongside providing psychological support to patients facing prolonged recovery periods. Mastery of these concepts forms the cornerstone of safe, evidence-based orthopedic nursing practice across various clinical settings.

headings.title: Hypovolemic Shock and Hemorrhage
headings.content: Hypovolemic shock and hemorrhage represent critical, life-threatening early complications of musculoskeletal injuries, especially those involving pelvic fractures and multiple long bone fractures like the femur. The femur is capable of sequestering up to 1.5 to 2 liters of blood within the surrounding thigh tissues upon fracturing, while pelvic ring disruptions can cause massive retroperitoneal bleeding due to the disruption of rich vascular networks and pelvic venous plexuses. As blood escapes the damaged vascular bed, circulating blood volume plummets, leading to decreased venous return, diminished cardiac output, and inadequate tissue perfusion. Clinical manifestations of hypovolemic shock include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, altered mental status, and delayed capillary refill. Nigerian nursing students must recognize that internal bleeding associated with orthopedic trauma can be insidious and may not be immediately obvious, as external wounds might appear minor. Initial emergency management focuses on restoring circulating volume through aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids and administration of blood products as prescribed. Simultaneously, healthcare providers must immobilize the fracture site to prevent further vascular tearing from jagged bone ends, apply pelvic binders if indicated, and prepare the patient for surgical stabilization or angiography for embolization. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, strict fluid balance tracking via an indwelling urinary catheter, and serial hemoglobin and hematocrit checks are essential nursing responsibilities in stabilizing these vulnerable patients.

headings.title: Fat Embolism Syndrome
headings.content: Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) is a serious and potentially fatal systemic condition that most frequently complicates fractures of long bones, particularly the femur and tibia, as well as pelvic fractures. FES occurs when fat globules are released from the bone marrow into the systemic circulation, where they lodge in small blood vessels of the lungs, brain, skin, and other organs. While asymptomatic fat embolization happens in many fracture cases, full-blown Fat Embolism Syndrome presents a classic clinical triad: respiratory distress, neurological impairment, and a distinct petechial rash. The respiratory symptoms stem from pulmonary capillary occlusion and inflammation, manifesting as tachypnea, hypoxemia, dyspnea, and tachycardia, which can rapidly progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Neurological signs range from restlessness, confusion, and lethargy to seizures and coma, caused by cerebral microemboli and hypoxia. A hallmark diagnostic sign, though it appears late, is a non-palpable petechial rash distributed across the chest, neck, axillae, and conjunctiva, resulting from small vessel occlusion and subsequent microhemorrhages. Nursing management for FES is primarily supportive and focuses on maintaining adequate oxygenation and ventilation through supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, stabilizing long bone fractures early to prevent further fat droplet release, ensuring adequate hydration, and administering corticosteroids if prescribed to reduce systemic inflammation. Vigilant respiratory and neurological assessment is paramount for early detection.

headings.title: Compartment Syndrome
headings.content: Compartment syndrome is a severe, limb-threatening surgical emergency characterized by increased pressure within a confined anatomical muscle compartment, leading to compromised blood flow, tissue ischemia, and eventual necrosis. Because muscle fascia is non-elastic, swelling or bleeding inside an enclosed compartment cannot expand outward; instead, internal pressure rises rapidly, crushing blood vessels and nerves. Common causes include tibial fractures, crush injuries, overly tight casts, circumferential burns, and prolonged limb compression. The hallmark clinical manifestation of compartment syndrome is severe, unrelenting pain that is disproportionate to the injury and completely unresponsive to opioid analgesics. Nursing students must remember the classic '5 Ps' of neurovascular assessment: Pain (out of proportion), Pallor, Paresthesia (early sign of nerve ischemia), Paralysis (a late, ominous sign indicating nerve and muscle death), and Pulselessness (an extremely late sign often indicating complete arterial occlusion). Pulses may remain palpable because capillary pressure is exceeded long before main arterial pressure is lost. Management requires immediate removal of any constrictive devices, such as splitting or removing casts and dressings, and keeping the extremity at the level of the heart—not elevated, as elevation reduces arterial perfusion pressure. If conservative measures fail, an emergency fasciotomy must be performed to surgically open the fascia, relieve pressure, and restore tissue perfusion.

headings.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
headings.content: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and its severe consequence, Pulmonary Embolism (PE), are major thromboembolic complications frequently encountered in immobilized orthopedic patients. Virchow's triad—venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability—explains the pathogenesis: orthopedic surgery, trauma, and prolonged bedrest create sluggish blood flow and activate the clotting cascade. A thrombus typically forms in the deep veins of the calf or thigh. While a DVT may present with unilateral calf swelling, warmth, tenderness, and a positive Homan's sign (though clinically unreliable), many cases are asymptomatic until a piece of the clot breaks loose, travels through the right side of the heart, and occludes the pulmonary arterial bed, becoming a pulmonary embolism. PE is a medical emergency manifesting abruptly with dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, apprehension, hemoptysis, and acute hypoxemia, potentially leading to sudden cardiovascular collapse and death. Nursing management centers heavily on prevention and early detection. Prophylactic measures include early ambulation, application of graduated compression stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression devices, and administration of anticoagulant medications such as low-molecular-weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, or direct oral anticoagulants as ordered. When PE is suspected, the nurse must immediately administer high-flow oxygen, elevate the head of the bed, notify the physician instantly, and prepare for emergency diagnostic imaging such as a CT pulmonary angiography and initiation of definitive anticoagulant or thrombolytic therapy.

headings.title: Osteomyelitis and Wound Infections
headings.content: Osteomyelitis is a severe, progressive bone infection that can complicate open fractures, surgical internal fixation procedures (orthopedic hardware implantation), or spread hematogenously from distant infection sites. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism responsible for bone infections. When bacteria invade the bone tissue and marrow, they trigger an inflammatory response that increases intraosseous pressure, leads to thrombosis of local blood vessels, and causes localized bone necrosis, resulting in the formation of sequestra (dead bone pieces) and involucrum (new bone formation around dead bone). Clinical manifestations of acute osteomyelitis include localized bone pain that worsens with activity and is unrelieved by rest, systemic fever, chills, night sweats, localized swelling, erythema, and warmth at the wound or fracture site. Chronic osteomyelitis features persistent draining sinuses and long-standing bone pain. Nursing care focuses heavily on stringent aseptic technique during surgical dressing changes and pin site care to prevent nosocomial introduction of pathogens. Once osteomyelitis is diagnosed, treatment requires prolonged antibiotic therapy—often lasting 4 to 6 weeks or longer—administered intravenously via peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs). Nurses must monitor for antibiotic side effects, ensure therapeutic drug levels, manage pain, encourage a high-protein and high-vitamin diet to promote wound healing and bone regeneration, and prepare the patient for potential surgical debridement of necrotic bone tissue.

headings.title: Avascular Necrosis
headings.content: Avascular necrosis (AVN), also known as osteonecrosis, occurs when there is a temporary or permanent loss of blood supply to the bones, resulting in cellular death of bone and marrow elements. Without adequate blood supply, the structural integrity of the bone collapses over time, leading to joint destruction and chronic functional impairment. Common sites affected include the femoral head (often following femoral neck fractures or hip dislocations due to disruption of the medial circumflex femoral artery), the scaphoid bone, and proximal humerus. Risk factors include severe traumatic fractures, joint dislocations, chronic corticosteroid therapy, excessive alcohol consumption, and sickle cell disease. In the early stages, AVN may be entirely asymptomatic, but as ischemia progresses and subchondral bone fractures or collapses, the patient experiences deep, throbbing pain that worsens with weight-bearing and movement, eventually resulting in restricted joint range of motion. Nursing students must recognize that patients with hip fractures or dislocations require long-term follow-up to detect early signs of AVN. Management depends on the stage of necrosis and can range from conservative approaches like activity modification, non-weight-bearing status using assistive devices, and pharmacotherapy, to surgical interventions such as core decompression to relieve pressure, bone grafting, osteotomy, or total joint replacement (arthroplasty) when joint destruction is advanced.

headings.title: Delayed Union, Malunion, and Nonunion
headings.content: Bone healing is a complex biological process that can sometimes fail or deviate from the normal timeline, resulting in delayed union, malunion, or nonunion. Delayed union refers to a fracture that takes substantially longer than the average expected time to heal—typically beyond 3 to 4 months—though there is still radiological and clinical evidence of ongoing healing progress. Malunion occurs when the fracture heals in an abnormal anatomical position, leading to cosmetic deformity, muscular imbalance, altered biomechanics, and long-term functional impairment or secondary osteoarthritis. Nonunion is the complete failure of the fracture ends to unite after 6 to 9 months, with no progressive radiological signs of healing; the fracture ends become rounded, sclerotic, and form a false joint, or pseudoarthrosis. Contributing factors to these healing complications include inadequate immobilization, excessive motion at the fracture site, poor local blood supply, severe soft tissue interposition between bone fragments, systemic malnutrition, smoking, and infection (osteomyelitis). Nursing care involves educating the patient on the critical importance of strict adherence to immobilization devices, activity restrictions, and nutritional support rich in calcium, vitamin D, and protein. Nurses also assist in preparing patients for electrical bone stimulation therapy, bone grafting procedures, or surgical revision with internal and external fixation when surgical intervention is required to correct nonunion or malunion.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Management of Musculoskeletal Complications
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment and management of musculoskeletal complications demand rigorous clinical vigilance, systematic data collection, and prompt intervention. The nurse serves as the frontline healthcare professional responsible for monitoring the patient's physical and psychological status throughout the recovery trajectory. Routine assessments must include serial neurovascular checks (checking peripheral pulses, capillary refill, skin color, temperature, sensation, and motor movement distal to the injury or cast), careful monitoring of vital signs to detect early indicators of hemorrhage, shock, or fat embolism, and diligent inspection of surgical incisions, wound dressings, and external fixation pin sites for signs of infection such as purulent drainage, foul odor, and spreading erythema. Pain management is paramount; nurses must differentiate between normal post-fracture discomfort and the agonizing, unrelenting pain characteristic of compartment syndrome. Effective management also involves implementing preventative measures against DVT and pressure injuries, encouraging deep breathing exercises to prevent atelectasis, maintaining prescribed traction or immobilization alignment, and ensuring optimal nutritional intake to support tissue repair and bone mineralization. Furthermore, nurses provide patient and family education regarding warning signs that necessitate immediate medical contact, psychological support for coping with prolonged immobility, and coordination with physical therapists for safe, progressive rehabilitation to restore optimal functional independence.
